pieces.title: Character art
pieces.brief:
You own how the kids look. This is the single biggest lever on whether the game feels like Backyard Baseball, so treat it as the marquee piece it is.

Build a parametric kid: the proportions from docs/BYB-REFERENCE.md (big head, short limbs, a silhouette a child could draw from memory), constructed so that every kid on the roster is the same rig with different dials — height, weight, head shape, posture, stance — and still reads as an individual at gameplay distance. Silhouette is the test: a critic must be able to tell two kids apart as black shapes.

Faces: eyes with actual character (pupils that look somewhere, lids that can narrow), eyebrows that carry most of the expression, a mouth vocabulary covering at least neutral, grin, gritted determination, shock, disappointment, taunt, and a wide-open yell. Faces must read at gameplay distance, which means bold shapes and high contrast, not fine detail. Provide an API other systems call — setExpression(kid, name) — because the animation and announcer pieces depend on it.

Wardrobe, straight from docs/PERIOD-REFERENCE.md and Backyard-ified: newsboy caps at various angles, flat caps, one kid in a too-big adult hat; knickerbockers, suspenders, rolled sleeves, patched knees, mismatched socks, worn boots, one kid barefoot, one in a hand-me-down jersey three sizes too big, one girl in a play dress with the hem taken up because she is faster than everybody. Two team identities that read instantly at distance (a colour on the cap or a sash or an armband — not full uniforms, these are street kids), while every kid still keeps their own clothes.

Hands must be able to hold a broom-handle bat and a Spaldeen, so build attach points the animation piece can parent to.

Diverse and specific: this is a 1925 New York block, so build the range the reference describes and give each kid a body language, not just a palette swap.

Register 'lineup' (all kids side by side in a neutral pose, front-lit, for silhouette and variety judging) and 'face_sheet' (close on several faces cycling expressions).

pieces.title: Animation vocabulary
pieces.brief:
You own everything the kids do. Backyard Baseball's aliveness is almost entirely animation, so nothing here may be a static pose.

Build a procedural animation system on top of the rig from src/chars/rig.js: a clip format, blending between clips, additive layers (a fidget that plays over an idle), timing curves with real anticipation and follow-through, squash and stretch, and secondary motion (hair, cap brim, shirt, the bat's whip).

The vocabulary, all of it: idle with fidgets that differ per kid (kicking a pebble, tugging the cap, chattering at the batter, spitting, hitching up pants); the batter's stance, waggle, stride, swing with a real weight shift and follow-through, the check swing, the whiff that spins them around; the pitcher's set, windup, leg kick, release and recovery; a run cycle with acceleration and a hard stop; a slide into a chalk base; a dive for a ball; a jump catch; a fumble; the throw; and the celebrations — the home-run trot, the jump, the arms-up, a taunt, a sulk, the whole team mobbing somebody at the plate.

Specific beats the design bible calls for must be animatable: the batter pointing at the fire escape before swinging, everyone freezing and scattering when somebody yells CAR, the argument where two kids get in each other's face.

Wire the kids into the game: src/chars/players.js places the fielders, the batter, the pitcher and the runners and drives their state from the sim's events on the bus, so animation always matches what the game says is happening.

Judge your own work with tools/film.mjs, not stills — read the contact sheets and fix anything that pops, slides, or holds a pose too long. Feet must not skate.

Register 'anim_idle', 'anim_swing', 'anim_run' and 'anim_celebrate', each composed so a critic can judge the motion from a frame strip.

pieces.title: Roster and personality
pieces.brief:
You own who these kids are. Backyard Baseball is loved because of Pablo Sanchez, not because of its physics — every kid must be somebody.

Write a roster of sixteen kids from a 1925 New York block, drawing names and neighbourhoods from docs/PERIOD-REFERENCE.md: Italian, Irish, Jewish, Black, Puerto Rican, Chinese, German, Polish families, boys and girls, ages eight to thirteen. Each gets: a real name and the nickname the block actually calls them, a one-line reputation, stats (power, contact, speed, arm, fielding, nerve) that make them good at something and bad at something else, a batting stance and a pitching quirk, a signature line they yell, a superstition, and a hidden trait the game can reveal (the quiet one who is the best hitter on the block; the little brother nobody picks who is untouchably fast; the kid whose mother calls him in at the worst possible moment).

One kid must be the Pablo Sanchez of this block — small, unassuming, absurdly good, universally beloved. Make the joke land without explaining it.

Build portraits procedurally in src/chars/portraits.js — canvas-drawn character cards in the period's illustration language (think a cigarette card or a hand-lettered lineup), one per kid, generated at load with no network fetch.

Build the team-select screen in src/ui/teamselect.js: pick-your-team the way it actually happened on a street, two captains alternating picks, the kids reacting to being picked or passed over, portraits and stats and the line they yell when chosen. It must be operable with keyboard, mouse and touch, and it must be funny.

Expose the roster to the rest of the game as data other systems read — the announcer piece will use the names and lines, the character-art piece reads the appearance dials, so define that shape clearly and document it at the top of roster.js.

Register 'team_select' and 'portrait_sheet'.
